input: In this worked example, we will explore how to estimate the steady-state conversion for a continuous stirred-tank reactor, often abbreviated as a CSTR, that is being used to carry out a neutralisation reaction. It is important to note that the reaction in question is first order in the limiting reactant, which means that the rate depends linearly on the concentration of that particular reactant, and this assumption forms the basis of the calculation that follows. The rate constant for the reaction, at the operating temperature of the system, is given as 0.139 min-1, and the mean residence time of material within the reactor is 37 min, so both of the key parameters needed for the ideal-reactor calculation are available. When these values are brought together in the standard design relation for an ideal CSTR, the steady-state conversion comes out at 83.7%, which represents the fraction of the limiting reactant that is converted under the assumed conditions. However, it is worth keeping in mind that this estimate rests on two important idealisations, namely perfect mixing throughout the vessel and constant density of the reacting mixture as the reaction proceeds. In a real vessel, mixing may not be perfectly uniform, and these assumptions should therefore be treated with a degree of caution. Furthermore, tracer tests, which would help to characterise the actual flow behaviour inside the vessel, have not been run on the actual vessel, so the idealised picture has not yet been checked against experimental evidence from the real system. The figure of 83.7% should therefore be read as the conversion predicted by the idealised model rather than as a measured outcome for the vessel itself.
target: A continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant at the operating temperature is 0.139 min-1 and the mean residence time is 37 min. For an ideal CSTR at steady state, these values give a conversion of the limiting reactant of 83.7%. Conversion here is the fraction of the limiting reactant converted in a single pass at steady state, and the result follows from the first-order rate law combined with the residence time in the standard CSTR design relation. Two idealisations carry the estimate. Perfect mixing is assumed, so the composition everywhere in the vessel equals the outlet composition, and density is taken as constant through the reaction. A real vessel departs from both: mixing is never complete, and a density change would alter the residence time at a fixed volumetric flow. The direction of the combined error is not fixed by the calculation itself. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run. A tracer test would measure the residence-time distribution of the real vessel and show how far it departs from the perfectly mixed case, so the 83.7% figure stands as an ideal-reactor estimate, uncorrected for the flow behaviour of the equipment in which the neutralisation would actually be carried out. The residence time enters the result directly: at fixed rate constant, a longer residence time raises conversion, and a shorter one lowers it, in the proportion the design relation sets.
